en: Regarding the general principles of bestowing food in the Esoteric Transmission, recorded by Sanfeng Fazang:

Without practicing Chan meditation, there is no means to awaken and enter; without awakening and entering, there is no means to penetrate deeply into the Dharma-gate. If one enters the Dharma, it must be done exhaustively.
Why forget the Dharma? If one forgets the Dharma, one lacks understanding; how then can there be function? Without great function, there is no way to achieve resonance.
If there is no resonance, how can one most effectively benefit sentient beings? There are many gates for benefiting sentient beings, yet every single gate possesses the seven matters mentioned above.
I have previously observed this in the single practice of the *Yankou Shishi* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts). This method is called Yoga, a term from the Sanskrit language.
*Yoga* is here translated as "correspondence" (*xiangying*). By means of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, one corresponds with the Dharma realized;

thus, great function manifests before one, giving rise to the path of vast benefit. This name truly accords with its reality. Generally speaking, the practice of *chan* (meditation) lies in thorough awakening;
to awaken to the Way, one must penetrate the essential principle (*zongzhi*). Once the essential principle is fully understood, then the immeasurable and diverse Dharma gates [will all be mastered].
All share the same essential intent. Thus, regarding the single dharma of offering food: from its essence arises its function;

it resides solely within this [circle], which possesses the heart-essence of the syllable *hrīḥ*. Upon this essence manifests the Flower Garland Dharma-realm (*Avataṃsaka-dharmadhātu*) of the syllables *pra* and *laṃ*, which are the conditions for the golden [light].
This Dharma-realm transforms into a palace, merging with the great trichiliocosm. However, this essence cannot easily be reached.
It is attained. Therefore, first, from the syllable *Oṃ-lam*, one severs [obstructions] at both ends, from the crown of the head to the navel.

With the hand, the mind, and the mouth reaching [the object], one purifies the *dharmadhātu* by means of the rite of sprinkling and purification. The *dharmadhātu* is the realm (*dhātu*) that possesses all phenomena (*dharma*).
Once the *dharmadhātu* is purified, its essence is already complete, yet its function has not yet been realized; therefore, one visualizes flowers and rice as the seeds of all phenomena. However...
The Dharma possesses both host and guest; it is simply compassion and majesty. Thus, the bell is used to discourse on compassion, while the vajra is employed for majesty.
As host and guest operate in tandem, they establish the *maṇḍala*. All musical instruments are the correct speech that expounds the Dharma, for they originate from the bell.
Upon awakening through the bell, one understands the incantations; upon awakening through the vajra, one understands the power of the incantations.
Thus, inconceivable matters are accomplished herein. To accomplish the supreme dharma, one must enter the Mahāyāna gate of non-substantiality via the twelve links of dependent origination.
Upon entering its initial gate, one proceeds from non-substantiality and dependent arising to the Bodhisattva’s simultaneous illumination and simultaneous negation. Roll!
Entering the Buddha-ground, the five Buddhas of the five directions manifest as the lords of the *dharmadhātu* to establish it.

Once the ground of the *dharmadhātu* is perfected, it is fundamentally the pure land within one's own nature. One should extensively shake it with the sound of the Avalokiteśvara of correct speech and seal it with the six-syllable heart mantra.
Within the infinite realms of the *dharmadhātu*, one points to and reveals a single realm to demonstrate the Great.

[The Buddha] said: "However, the realms emerge from this. Within this, the movement of a single moment of activity becomes the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). When it moves, it flows, and thus becomes the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*).

When the flow reaches its limit, it becomes solid, and thus becomes the gold-circle (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*). When the solidity reaches its limit, it becomes turbid, and thus becomes the earth-circle (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*).
Therefore, the Cakravāḍa, the Cakravāḍa-iron mountains, the Great Sumeru, the Small Sumerus, the four great continents, and the eight [subcontinents] are established."
The auxiliary continents and the minor scattered islands are covered above by a parasol of various jewels and established below by a banner of supreme victory;
thus the eight treasures of the wheel-turning king are complete, and the sun, moon, stars, and heavens are complete.
This vajra-ground emerges from the ground of the supreme vajra-base within true nature, arising from the syllable *HŪṂ*. How could it be something established by ignorance? Within this nature—
From each of the flowers and grains upon the ground, one extracts palaces, gardens, ponds, parasols, banners, and other such objects;
all of these flow forth from within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as offerings. All incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, fruits, and so forth—
Joy represents the six *pāramitās* as its great function. With the true speech (*samyag-vāk*) of the bell and *vajra*, one makes a universal proclamation.

Within this—specifically within that true speech—one extracts the drum of the three poisons to form a three-pointed wheel of fire, and extracts the jewel lattice to form the seed-syllable of the wish-fulfilling gem.
Within this, one visualizes the yellow syllable *Dlaṃ*, which emits yellow light.

This manifests the color of ultimate benefit to illuminate and care for sentient beings. With a single thought of turning the light back upon itself, the original character transforms into Ratnasambhava Buddha.

His hands form the mudrā of generosity (*varada-mudrā*), holding a jewel lattice to extensively accomplish the benefit of giving. Whenever one intends to bestow benefit, the very mind of giving becomes an obstacle;
it must therefore be eliminated by employing the methods of "slaying the Buddhas and patriarchs. Thus, first, with three points...

The fire burns through once and enters into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). However, emptiness is also an obstruction. Therefore, one uses the poison-fists of the double vajra, crossing them correctly, to release fire and burn it again.
Yet, the total exhaustion of emptiness is also an obstruction. Furthermore, one must burn it with the fire of external, mutually intersecting power.
Once emptiness is exhausted, that very "exhaustion" is itself an object of cognition; how could it not be an obstruction? Therefore, by means of the inner vajra...
It is incinerated by flames. Generally, whenever a single dharma is established, there arises a "demon" of that dharma consisting of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
One must use the fire of the power of these four-proposition dharmas to burn it away; only then will the great *maṇḍala* (great circle) aspect of the fundamental essence be seen.

This aspect originally emerges from the heart of the syllable *Hrīḥ*. Being without [discursive] mind, all things are accomplished as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) through a single thought-moment of the seed-syllable *Praṃ* arising from the heart.
Therefore it is said: within emptiness, one visualizes *laṃ* (*laṃ*) and *pam* (*pam*). Yet, although *pam* is beginningless, the sound of the beginningless arises from *a*;
since even that does not exist, existence arises from non-existence.
Thus, all phenomena emerge from *hūṃ*, thereby forming the worlds of the ten directions by flowing forth as fragrant flowers and so on. Now, regarding these flowers:
The incense and other offerings arise from the syllable *HŪṂ*. This is the syllable *Sukṣma*, the unattainable heaven. That heaven naturally has a Mother. The Mother has four arms;
they rise together and fall together. The upper two hold flowers; the lower two are joined in a wheel (*cakra*). The marvel lies in the four-armed wheel-union:
opening and closing together, it is utterly ungraspable, yet through this, this Dharma is accomplished. How could the mind-consciousness of an ordinary person [comprehend] this?
It is that which has arrived; it is that which arrives at the place where arrival is impossible. Because its power and function are grave and solemn, there is the syllable *Oṃ*.

When its power and function are first complete, this *dharmadhātu* is fully present. Therefore, the various phenomena in the upper fascicle do not exceed the matters concerning the subtle manifestation of the Great Wheel Vidyārāja.
As for its mudrā: the outer fingers cross while the inner fingers point outward and are concealed. This precisely manifests this *dharmadhātu*.
It is the secret (*guhya*). Now that this *dharmadhātu* has been established, the Buddha-mind appears within it;
therefore, with the two vajra-poison-fists, the four fingers of the front and back hands interlace their strength. This is the secret place of the mind.
When this secret place slightly vibrates, the syllable *hrīḥ* emits light that reaches the Akaniṣṭha realm, inviting the wisdom-form of Avalokiteśvara himself to transform my physical form.
Body. This seeing-mind’s light shines through all forms; wherever it reaches upon any form, it arrives at the ultimate limit, which is called the "place of ultimate reality.
This is none other than my own body, Avalokiteśvara. To request his arrival and exchange with my body means that "I" am no longer "I.
Ultimately, by taking full responsibility for oneself, one gives rise to the pride of being Avalokiteśvara; one is oneself the Lord of the Great Dharma-realm, namely Vairocana.

That person sat entirely within the sovereign *prajñā*, and thus silently recited the Heart Sūtra. As for me, beneath my seat there was a great lotus flower with hundreds of thousands of millions of petals;
from each and every petal, a Buddha appeared, each of whom was a transformation Buddha presiding over his own assembly of disciples and protective deities, facing me directly.
My body had four faces, each facing a Buddha, so that the principal and the retinue were gathered together. Thus it was.

The Buddhas are none other than my own transformation bodies; thus, Avalokiteśvara emits light to invite the Buddhas. Once the Buddhas have arrived, one extends the six offerings to worship them—this is the practice of Samantabhadra.
One then employs the mind that forms the *uṣṇīṣa* [crown] as an offering, signifying the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
As soon as the thought of making an offering arises, it is itself a mental demon (*cittamāra*); therefore, one continues with the three points and the three seals.
Burn it. Offer this by transforming it into the signlessness of emptiness; all of this does not transcend the syllables *HŪṂ* and *OṂ*.

Although it has been transformed into emptiness, one has not yet entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). This still belongs to the merit of the wisdom of vision (*darśana-jñāna*). One must enter the concentrations of hearing, reflection, and cultivation to perfect the Great Wisdom (*mahā-prajñā*).
Therefore, within that concentration, with eyes closed and the mind clarified, one visualizes within the body, at the tip of the fleshy heart-center.
Above, visualize a red syllable *baṃ*. It transforms into an eight-petaled lotus of variegated colors.
Upon the flower, visualize a white syllable *a*, which transforms into a perfectly round and pure white form, like the full moon. Within this essence...
Visualize the heart-seal of the syllable *hrīḥ* emitting light; the light transforms into an eight-petaled lotus flower to symbolize the eight consciousnesses.

Upon the flower appears the Bodhisattva Īśvara as the Sovereign King of Unobstructed Mind. The Bodhisattva holds the flower with his left hand, while his right hand makes the gesture of opening the flower’s petals.
This signifies that cause and effect, as well as phenomena and principle, mutually conceal and reveal one another in order to deliver sentient beings. This...
The "flower" refers to the mind-flower that emerges separately from above the self-Buddha of the eight consciousnesses; this is that which every person inherently possesses.

Therefore, when Bodhisattvas contemplate sentient beings, they see that each one possesses this flower and is fundamentally a Buddha from the very beginning, never having failed to awaken to this truth.
Viewed in this light, the Dharma-realm is originally pure; how could there be any delusion or defilement? It is simply the consciousness-mind of every person.
Within the midst of feelings and perceptions, each consciousness possesses one Tathāgata.

Since every ordinary person’s mind-consciousness contains a Tathāgata, how could their moving minds and distracted thoughts ever fail to be in samādhi? Therefore, the eight Tathāgatas all enter samādhi together within the sovereign mind.
The light shines with brilliant clarity. Although these flowers are small within the minds of sentient beings, they are in no way different from those of the Buddha.

Therefore, as the flowers gradually unfold, each reaches a magnitude that encompasses the entire Dharma-realm. The flowers of sentient beings are identical to those in the ocean-like assembly of the Buddha;
all are of one mind, without self or other. Because their own minds do not shift yet they take pity upon sentient beings, [the flowers of] sentient beings—
The flowers, illuminated by the light of Mengzi, are all liberated from suffering and affliction; they become identical with my own mind.

The flowers that have unfolded gradually withdraw and contract the *dharmadhātu*, becoming equal in measure to oneself. Having withdrawn them into the secret treasury, one again forms the seal of the Sovereign Avalokiteśvara.
Once they have returned to a single body, one performs empowerment upon the four places. First, the syllable *Oṃ* is added to the mouth, and next, with...
Place the syllable *HŪṂ* at the crown of the head; place the syllable *DRAṂ* at the navel; place the syllable *HRĪḤ* at the heart;
and again, place the syllable *A* at the throat. Roll these back into a single mind. Furthermore, make each part of the body—the mouth, crown, heart, and navel—individually firm and stable.
This is the ultimate limit of meditative concentration, a realm that cannot be reached by the ordinary mind. Upon entering this concentration, one becomes...
This inconceivable power is capable of shattering the iron mountains, the firm darkness of hell. This mudrā is the symbol of the firmness of the Iron Mountains;
furthermore, it is the symbol of the firmness of entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), for these two are not distinct.

As he prepares to destroy hell, Avalokiteśvara manifests a great majestic presence, his entire body crimson in color. From the tip of his tongue, his fingers in the mudrā, and his heart and mouth, he emits light.
Red light emanates from the three places [of the body]. With both hands in vajra-fists, the hands hook downward and point upward, forming the gesture of shattering hell.
Reciting the empowerment mantra, the light touches the hells, and the hells are instantly shattered. These hells were created by the deluded actions of the three karmas of sentient beings;
now, through the true power of the Dharma of the three karmas, they are shaken and destroyed, vanishing in an instant. Furthermore, there is no duality here.
Nevertheless, hell is the Buddha-mind; how could it not have a presiding lord? Therefore, when the hells are destroyed, Kṣitigarbha emerges.
Having completed the five offerings to Kṣitigarbha, one then transforms the previous red light of majesty into white light of compassion.
From the syllable *hṛīḥ* within the left hand, light is emitted, beckoning those of the six realms into the ritual arena.
He circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated, and withdrew. Upon reaching the altar, he divided [the assembly] into six sections and settled them there.

Once they were settled, he applied the Seal of Firmness (*dṛḍhamudrā*) upon the syllable *Hṛdaya* (the Great Compassionate Heart) from which light issued forth, entering the crowns of the heads of those in the six realms of existence.

This caused the mists of their transgressions to manifest throughout their entire bodies. Once the manifestations of their offenses had appeared, they were bound together to form mountains of sin, which were then colored with shifting shades of blue and green.
Avalokiteśvara, with his two fingers, rubbed and moved the golden syllable *taraṭa*; with a single sound, he shattered that mountain into something like fine dust.
As for those karmic deeds whose results are irreversible, these do not involve severing the mind that perceives cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Since it is impossible to exhaustively empty [all karma], one therefore uses the *hṛdaya* seal upon the moon of the mind to emit blue light that illuminates all those who have committed offenses.
Because the offenses for which even the thousand Buddhas cannot provide absolution arise from the notion of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), they are extinguished within that pure nature.
Thus, the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without distinction, and fixed karma has no place to settle. Furthermore, by means of the white-colored mind...
The various rays of light enter the bodies of those who have committed offenses, like the sun evaporating dew. Their black karma emerges from their feet and flows down to the vajra-limit;
this is called "confession and purification. Once each has been purified, they merely regain their original essence, yet it is not yet fully adorned.
Therefore, they are further drenched with the nectar of the wondrous form-body within the syllable *hrīḥ* in the formless realm.
Visualize a blue lotus flower; this flower is the wondrous mind. Within the flower is a white letter *A*, which is the midst of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
From within the letter, the water of nature flows forth, which the hungry ghosts swallow and receive with refreshing clarity and without obstruction.

They then ascend to the ground of precious victory, remaining free from fear. Attaining a vast and expansive body, they realize the wondrous form-body (*rūpakāya*), becoming richly adorned with many jewels, until they reach [the ultimate goal].
Immeasurable light returns to the vast majestic power and sovereign radiance that enters the world. All things are unimpeded;
one takes refuge in self-nature, which is fully endowed with the Three Jewels, and gives rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are thus three things without distinction; they are fused into a lunar disc, perfectly pure and unsurpassed.
Within it is a golden letter A, as fine as the tip of an autumn hair, appearing yet vanishing, such that it cannot be apprehended in four ways.
There is no Buddha to be realized; there is no birth to be delivered from; there are no practices to be cultivated.

When one does not know what birth-and-death or nirvana are, and with a single step one falls [into realization], one immediately attains the true precepts. What has been described above is still merely the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*); their functional application has not yet been achieved.

Therefore, within the seal there is the white syllable *VAM*, which emits light that universally illumines sentient beings. Only when the precepts are thus perfected is universal enlightenment (*samantabhadra*) realized.

The body of virtuous conduct, within the lunar disc, succeeds to the office of all Buddhas. Only upon reaching this stage of realization is one worthy of receiving the food of the true sustenance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

how could it be merely fruit-food? The previous state of mind regarding the precepts was entirely devoid of a single thought, yet now, in bestowing this food, there is once again the presence of the mind;
therefore, Māra is again dispatched to transform it into emptiness. From within that emptiness, a hand emerges, red in color and majestic in its power.
The syllable *baṅ* transforms into the lotus of the non-attainment of the three—emptiness, conventionality, and the middle—at the center of the majestic mandala.
Visualize that it becomes the syllable *vaṃ*, pure white in color. From within its bindu, there flow forth food and drink of wondrous petals, arising from non-existence;
these are scattered as infinite offerings in Magadhan measures, becoming immeasurable nectar and an ocean of milk, butter, and curd.

All the hosts of spirits have been fully satiated with food obtained through right livelihood. Furthermore, as for those hosts of obstructing spirits who previously hindered offerings, they have each been burned away by the fire of wisdom and compelled to retreat;
thus, this supreme and excellent condition has been established. Now that this superior condition has been fulfilled, [the merit is complete].

Could it be that those who obstruct the giving to hungry ghosts are external objects not encompassed by the mind? Rather, one takes all the aforementioned seed-syllables (*akṣara-bīja*) as nectar and sprinkles them one by one upon all obstructing ghosts.

From the Three Jewels themselves down to the Earth Store Bodhisattva, and extending through the six realms of existence to the obstructing ghosts, each category is benefited accordingly, so that all together return to supreme *bodhi*. At this point, there is universal and equal offering.

Ordinary beings and sages share a single source; this is further subsumed within the syllable *hūṃ*. One performs a vast dedication of merit, ultimately returning to the syllable *a* as the great circular mandala (*maṇḍala*). Alas!

Beginning from the essence of the syllable *a*, which is the emptiness of the Great Sign, one perceives the fundamental mind of *he-ri* (*hrīḥ*). From within that mind, the Great Dharma Realm of *pūṃ* and *hūṃ* arises.
The ten thousand dharmas of *HŪṂ*: within each and every dharma, there is nothing apart from the vajra power and function of the syllable *OṂ*.
Ultimately firm and solid, it is primordially thus. How could there be any distinction between the Buddhas and sentient beings, or between nirvāṇa and saṃsāra?
It is because we, through a single moment of deluded ignorance, have fallen into saṃsāra, wandering about without knowing where to turn for refuge; therefore, the Guru...
It points out the Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs, causing one to return to the root and revert to the source, severing the continuity of past and future.
It restores the *oṃ* (*oṃkāra*) within the *hrīḥ* syllable at the middle finger; therein one perceives the Mind-Only that is neither obtainable nor unobtainable.
Within the mind, *phat* and *baṃ* manifest, encompassing heaven and earth like a lid covering a box; *hūṃ* is presented to bring forth immeasurable functions, following the waves.
"Chasing the waves": by adding *oṃ* to each and every dharma, one cuts off all currents. This essential principle is entirely the technique of Linji and Yunmen;

only then can the Way that benefits all without seeking benefit be widely propagated. Furthermore, this principle originated from the successive transmission of the patriarchs of the Western Regions and flowed eastward to reach National Teacher Huizhong.
After three transmissions, it became the essential principle of Yangshan. It is fully [contained therein].
There are ninety-seven [instances of] the zero-sign. Thus we know that the single dharma of offering food briefly reveals the function of resonance.

Is not the essential meaning of Zen meditation, then, a great matter of causal conditions? Truly, because this dharma has long been lost to its fundamental principle, it is only now, through investigating the teachings of the Five Houses, that we arrive at it.
Alas! Those who take directness as their school—upon hearing of these signs, what will they say?
Regarding the intent of this response, how could it fail to move one’s inner being?

The dharma of bestowing food is fundamentally the compassionate activity of the Tathāgata; yet, as the tradition has been lost over time, it has ultimately become akin to the performances of actors and singers.
Interspersed with songs, it was vulgar and unrefined, yet the subtle essence of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) was left entirely unaddressed—alas, how lamentable!

(Zang) At the age of twenty, I received this Dharma among the multitude; at twenty-nine, I studied the precepts with profound resolve, vowing to offer a hundred lecture halls as a gift to form the karmic conditions for Bodhisattvahood.
By chance, beneath my seat, a thousand lamps appeared, startling all who witnessed it.

[The work was] dispersed. Reflecting that the fires of grievous resentment could not be extinguished by anything other than the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), he thus vowed to cease [the project].
However, after more than ten years of practicing Zen, various spirits rose up and petitioned him in his dreams on more than one occasion.

Only then did he remember that his former vow remained unfulfilled; he then examined the original woodblock editions of the *Shiji* (Stone Machine) and verified them against the corrections made by Yunqi.

Having minutely investigated and contemplated the principles, I have integrated them with the five schools of Zen. Subsequently, I exhorted practitioners of both the scholastic and meditative traditions to observe these closely and practice them with diligence.
Thus, I have long ago committed to writing several folios of the "General Principles for the Bestowal of Food" (*śrāddha*).

At that time, the scholar Wang Chanzhao respectfully requested me to perform a ritual according to the Dharma for the benefit of his late father, Mr. Jihe. Upon seeing this, I was delighted and agreed to conduct the service as prescribed.
I have therefore carved this portion of my offerings onto printing blocks to widely announce it to those who have truly resolved to attain the bodhicitta and study the method of bestowing food.
If everyone contemplates these offerings according to the Dharma, then all hearts will be in accord upon the nine lotus flowers.
I request that you, Mr. Jihe, verify this from afar. At this time—
Recorded by Sanfeng (Fazang) on the [blank] day of the first month in the sixth year of the Tianqi era.
